description: Historical and contextual entities referenced by Books I–VI. These records are separate from narrative presence: the local novel corpus supplies the trigger, while authoritative external sources supply concise historical context. first_section is a global spoiler threshold.

book2_exclusions.reason: Historical school context exists, but the exact personal identity and chronology used by the novel were not supported strongly enough by an authoritative one-to-one source.
The reference is legendary/literary; it was not converted into a historical-person record.
Mentioned sword figures were not promoted without a sufficiently specific institutional identity record for the exact person named by this translation.
The local text does not resolve the individual securely enough for a canonical contextual entity.
These are retained as narrative characters; no historical status was inferred from name or institutional association.
Handled as an active narrative character. The micro-wiki adds the independently sourced Hōzōin-ryū institution rather than merging external biography into his scene record.

book3_exclusions.reason: Mentioned historical roster not promoted in this pass without a sufficiently specific institutional source for every exact identity used by the translation.
Sword and court figures remain narrative mentions because the exact translated identity was not validated one-to-one by an institutional authority.
Retained only as a narrative character; no authoritative source resolved the exact spelling, and it is deliberately not merged with Arakida Ujitsune or Arakida Moritake.
The chapter repeats shrine tradition; the traditional claim is not converted into independently established history.
Their equivalence is narrative evidence only and remains hidden until the explicit section-28 reveal.
Matahachi's claim is an impersonation; the dead bearer remains unidentified, and carrying the certificate is not proof of the bearer's identity.

book4_exclusions.reason: The exact identities named by the translation were not promoted without a sufficiently specific institutional authority in the validated Book IV source set.
Retained as narrative characters; no historical status is inferred from names, family association or setting.
A mocking mistaken name used by Kojirō in section 52 and immediately rejected by Matahachi; it is not a temporal identity or durable alias.
Official place sources validate site history or later tradition only, not the novel's combat details, participants or geometry.
The novel supports an emotional and artistic affinity by section 41 but does not establish a sexual union or documentary historical meeting.

book5_exclusions.reason: Narrative or unresolved places remain coordinate-free; broad historical context does not establish exact scene points.
Names are represented only at their progressive narrative windows and are not promoted to spoiler-prone global aliases.
The abduction is not allowed to overwrite the earlier relationship history, and Hyōgo's unspoken affection is not made reciprocal.
Retrospective reports remain references and do not create present-time physical movement or co-presence.

names: private residences, narrative cabins, teahouses and ambush sites
book6_exclusions.reason: Broad area history cannot establish exact fictional or private scene points; these locations remain coordinate-free.

book6_exclusions.reason: Niiza City associates the documented development with the 1655 canal works, so the translated place name is retained but mapping remains blocked as a possible anachronism.
The pouch and flute create a strong reader inference in section 96, but the chapter does not give Iori an explicit identification or reunion; no canonical relationship is published.

names: private houses, inns, caves, roads and exact shoreline scenes
book7_exclusions.reason: Institutional and municipal sources support only broad place context; all unresolved narrative sites remain coordinate-free.
Temporary and unrevealed names are represented by section-bounded identity windows, not spoiler-prone global aliases.
The pair explicitly acknowledge one another as husband and wife, but the novel states no civil or institutional ceremony.

names: Matahachi as biological father of Akemi's baby
book7_exclusions.reason: Matahachi chooses and enacts social fatherhood; the text deliberately leaves biological paternity unresolved.

names: Funashima duel tradition as proof of novel choreography
book7_exclusions.reason: Official local material preserves the 1612 tradition while noting variant accounts; it does not authenticate the novel's dialogue, timing strategy or exact blows.

entities.name: Kobayakawa Hideaki
entities.summary: Daimyo who defected from the Western Army at Sekigahara and attacked Otani Yoshitsugu's forces, contributing decisively to Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory.

entities.name: Ishida Mitsunari
entities.summary: Toyotomi administrator and principal leader of the Western coalition at Sekigahara, defeated by Tokugawa Ieyasu's coalition.

entities.name: Ukita Hideie
entities.summary: Major Toyotomi ally and commander of a large Western Army contingent at Sekigahara.

entities.name: Shimazu Yoshihiro
entities.summary: Satsuma daimyo and commander of the Shimazu contingent at Sekigahara, later noted for the retreat through the Eastern Army.

entities.name: Konishi Yukinaga
entities.summary: Christian daimyo and Western Army commander at Sekigahara who was captured after the defeat and executed.

entities.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
entities.summary: Leader of the Eastern Army at Sekigahara whose victory enabled the consolidation of Tokugawa political power.

entities.name: Minamoto no Hiromasa
entities.summary: Heian-period court musician, calligrapher and celebrated flute player, remembered in a medieval anecdote involving a mysterious flute player at Suzaku Gate in Kyoto.

entities.name: Akamatsu clan
entities.summary: A samurai clan based in Harima that became prominent as a shugo-daimyo family during the Muromachi period; Book I connects the Shimmen family to the Akamatsu lineage.

entities.name: Akamatsu Masanori
entities.summary: Akamatsu Masanori was a medieval Japanese military lord and shugo who restored the Akamatsu family's position in Harima, Bizen and Mimasaka during the Muromachi period. Book I invokes him in its account of the Shimmen family's Akamatsu lineage.

entities.name: Battle of Sekigahara
entities.summary: Decisive battle between Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern coalition and the Western coalition associated with the Toyotomi cause. The Western defeat transformed the political balance of Japan.

entities.name: Eastern Army
entities.summary: Coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu during the Sekigahara campaign of 1600.

entities.name: Western Army
entities.summary: Coalition associated with the Toyotomi cause and commanded at Sekigahara by Ishida Mitsunari and allied daimyo.

entities.name: The Art of War (Sunzi)
entities.period: traditionally attributed to the late 6th–5th century BCE; exact composition date disputed
entities.summary: Ancient Chinese military treatise traditionally attributed to Sunzi (Sun Tzu). Book I invokes it as a model of strategy and military thought, making the work itself part of the historical context rather than a character or faction.

entities.name: Oda Nobunaga
entities.summary: Military leader named in Book II's account of Kyoto's recent political past.

entities.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
entities.summary: Ruler and kanpaku named as Nobunaga's successor in Book II's political chronology.

entities.name: Tokugawa Hidetada
entities.summary: Second Tokugawa shogun, named when the novel describes Ieyasu's transfer of the title.

entities.name: Toyotomi Hideyori
entities.summary: Hideyoshi's heir, named at Osaka Castle in Book II's explanation of Tokugawa–Toyotomi tension.

entities.name: Okuni's kabuki-odori
entities.summary: Early-seventeenth-century Kyoto performance tradition associated with Okuni and named as popular entertainment in Book II.
sources: National Theatre of Japan / Japan Arts Council

entities.name: Yagyū Muneyoshi (Sekishūsai)
entities.summary: Historically documented Yagyū master who is first discussed in Book II before becoming an active narrative character.

entities.name: Yagyū Munenori
entities.summary: Sekishūsai's fifth son and later first Yagyū daimyo; Book II reports him away in Edo rather than physically present.

entities.name: Hōzōin-ryū sōjutsu
entities.summary: Spear tradition whose official lineage names Hōzōin Kakuzenbō Hōin In'ei as founder.

entities.name: Kamiizumi Nobutsuna (Lord Ise-no-kami)
entities.summary: Sword master linked with the Yagyū tradition; Book II's translated 'Lord Kōizumi of Ise' is normalized cautiously to this historical context.

entities.name: Fushimi castle town and port
entities.summary: Kyoto City's history describes Fushimi as a road-and-water transport hub shaped by Hideyoshi's castle construction and port development. This supports the broad setting, not the novel's exact worksite.

entities.name: Sasaki Kojirō
entities.summary: The National Diet Library maintains a personal-name authority for Sasaki Kojirō as a swordsman and records 1612 as his death year. The novel's biography, certificate and encounters remain literary evidence.

entities.name: Sumiyoshi Taisha
entities.summary: The shrine's official chronology supports its long historical presence at Sumiyoshi while noting scholarly debate around its traditional foundation date. It does not authenticate the novel's inn or shoreline scenes.

entities.name: Tsukahara Bokuden
entities.summary: Kashima City's cultural-property material identifies Bokuden as a historical swordsman born in 1489 and describes traditions associated with his training. The anecdotes repeated by the novel remain narrative context.

entities.name: Ise Jingū (Naikū)
entities.summary: Official Jingū material identifies Naikū and the Uji Bridge over the Isuzugawa at its entrance. This supports the general geography without fixing narrative scene coordinates.

entities.name: Karasumaru Mitsuhiro
entities.summary: Institutional catalogues identify Karasumaru Mitsuhiro (1579–1638) as a court noble and writer. His role, residence and commissions in the novel are not treated as documentary biography.
sources: Agency for Cultural Affairs / Cultural Heritage Online

entities.name: Great Gojō Bridge
entities.summary: Kyoto City's official chronology records construction of the Great Gojō Bridge in 1589. This supports the bridge's period existence, not the exact position of the novel's posted announcement or encounters.

entities.name: Hon'ami Kōetsu
entities.summary: Kyoto National Museum describes Kōetsu as a calligrapher and maker in lacquer and ceramics from the Hon'ami sword-polishing and appraisal family. The meetings with Musashi remain literary scenes.

entities.name: Rengeōin / Sanjūsangendō
entities.summary: The temple's official history confirms the Rengeōin/Sanjūsangendō identity, its twelfth-century foundation and later rebuilding. It does not validate the novel's duel with Denshichirō.

entities.name: Yoshino Tayū
entities.summary: Kyoto's official travel material preserves the cultural memory of the celebrated early-seventeenth-century Yoshino Tayū and associates her with Jōshōji. The novel's Yanagimachi setting and meetings may involve literary compression.

entities.name: Ichijōji Sagarimatsu
entities.summary: Kyoto's official guide identifies the old traffic point and presents the Musashi–Yoshioka episode as a famous legend; the present pine is a later generation. This is not independent proof of the novel's battle.

entities.name: Enryakuji
entities.summary: Enryakuji's official history records Nobunaga's 1571 destruction and a gradual reconstruction chronology. That supports broad period context only; Musashi's stay and the disciplinary hearing remain narrative.

entities.name: Seta no Karahashi
entities.summary: The Ōtsu tourism authority identifies Seta no Karahashi as a real and historically prominent bridge. It validates the locality label, not Musashi's rendezvous.
sources: Biwako Otsu Travel Guide / Otsu Tourism Association

entities.name: Otaki and Metaki waterfalls
entities.summary: Nagiso Tourism Association identifies the two waterfalls near the Tsumago–Magome route with the Musashi–Otsū episode in Yoshikawa's novel. This validates the intended literary location, not historical biography or exact early-Edo routing.

entities.name: Fukushima checkpoint on the Nakasendō
entities.summary: Kiso Town identifies Fukushima as one of the major Edo-period checkpoints and a transport junction. This supports the broad locality, not the novel's precise passage geometry.

entities.name: Narai-juku
entities.summary: Shiojiri City documents Narai as a Nakasendō post-town settlement along the Narai River. Daizō's premises and the novel's exact movements remain unmapped.

entities.name: Shimosuwa post town
entities.summary: Shimosuwa Town describes the locality as the junction of the Nakasendō and Kōshū routes, a hot-spring post town and a Suwa shrine gateway. The novel's inn and local route are not pinpointed.

entities.name: Mount Takao Yakuōin and Hachiōji
entities.summary: Hachiōji City's cultural material supports Mount Takao and Yakuōin as a longstanding religious setting. It does not locate the novel's inn, moat or burial mound.

entities.name: Early Edo, Nihombashi and the Sumida
entities.summary: Tokyo public authorities document the broad early-Edo development chronology and historical Sumida context. Private homes, ferry points and individual narrative routes remain unresolved.
sources: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Bureau of Construction

entities.name: Sensōji / Asakusa Kannon
entities.summary: Sensōji's official history supports the institution's continuity and Sumida origin tradition. The donation plaque and the novel's boat journey remain narrative claims.

entities.name: Kanda Myōjin
entities.summary: The shrine's official history documents its early-Edo relocations and enshrinement tradition. Daizō's reported donation is not independently authenticated.

entities.name: Tone River early-modern works
entities.summary: MLIT describes the early-modern eastward diversion of the Tone as a long sequence of works tied to flood control, new fields and transport. This does not identify fictional Hōtengahara.

entities.name: Azabu and Iigura
entities.summary: Minato City documents Azabu and Iigura as historical place names. The novel's Yagyū residence and Iori's precise route are not geolocated from this correspondence.

entities.name: Akagi shrine and Ushigome
entities.summary: Shinjuku City's cultural register supports the Akagi shrine tradition in Ushigome while cautioning that parts of the received chronology are estimated. The Hōjō house remains unmapped.

entities.name: Takanawa and Isarago
entities.summary: Minato City's district history documents Takanawa and the Edo-period Isarago place name. It does not locate the novel's cemetery or private lodging.

entities.name: Tanashi
entities.summary: Nishitokyo City's history supports Tanashi as an old locality name. The novel's overnight stop remains an unlocated narrative site.

entities.name: Kotesashigahara battlefield
entities.summary: Tokorozawa City identifies Kotesashigahara as a battlefield of the 1333 Kamakura campaign. This supports only the broad battlefield context, not the novel's bones or walking route.

entities.name: Mitsumine Shrine
entities.summary: Chichibu City's guide describes Mitsumine Shrine as a mountain-worship site at about 1,100 metres. It does not validate the novel's treasure theft, lodging or ambush route.

entities.name: Former Edo Castle complex
entities.summary: The Imperial Household Agency identifies the present palace grounds and East Gardens with the former Edo Castle complex. No modern point is substituted for the novel's Fukiage, woodshed or prison scenes.

entities.name: Nobidome historical warning
entities.summary: Niiza City's account ties Nobidome canal and village development to 1655. Because that is later than the narrative frame, the translated locality is preserved without a mapped point.

entities.name: Wadakura Gate
entities.summary: Chiyoda City's official planning material lists Wadakura Gate among Edo Castle remains. The novel's Reception Pavilion and Orchid Room remain unresolved narrative interiors.

entities.name: Kōfukuji
entities.summary: Kōfukuji's official history supports its long institutional continuity in Nara. The boys' contest and surrounding encounters remain literary scenes.

entities.name: Amanosan Kongōji
entities.summary: Kawachinagano City documents Amanosan Kongōji and its Nyonin Kōya tradition. The memorial visit, image association and ambush are narrative evidence only.

entities.name: Mount Kōya sacred landscape
entities.summary: UNESCO documents Kōyasan within the Kii sacred-sites and pilgrimage landscape. The novel's private political meeting and Mount Kudo network are not independently historicized.

entities.name: Sakai maritime trade and port
entities.summary: Sakai City describes the city as a medieval and early-modern trade hub. The Kobayashi premises, individual ships and passenger movements remain novel evidence.

entities.name: Himeji and Shikama
entities.summary: Himeji City supports the broad historical-city setting. It does not locate the novel's dyer household, cave, inn or exact estuary scene.

entities.name: Kokura under the Hosokawa
entities.summary: Kitakyushu public cultural material dates Hosokawa Tadaoki's major Kokura Castle construction to 1602 and records the city's Musashi–Kojirō association. Private meetings and duel administration remain literary.
sources: Kitakyushu City Time and Wind Museum

entities.name: Funashima / Ganryū-jima duel tradition
entities.summary: Shimonoseki City's official tourism material identifies Funashima with Ganryū-jima and preserves a 1612 duel tradition while explicitly noting variant accounts. The novel's choreography is not treated as archival fact.
